processing: Today a green tea made into tight, downy strips, across a range of grades from bud-rich top lots to everyday green. Exact steps are not published.
harvest_season: No picking calendar is published; as with other Chongqing mountain greens, spring is the usual and most valued season.
appearance_dry: Tight, well-made strips with visible white down and whole, glossy leaves.
appearance_wet: Whole leaves that open gracefully in the water.
taste_profile: Clean aroma and a mellow, sweet taste that brings up saliva and lingers.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a downy green rather than a local rule: water just below boiling suits it, and a glass lets you watch the leaves open. It is said to stand up to repeated steeping.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens it is sold by the current year's harvest and is best within about a year. The range runs from top bud grades to everyday green and even jasmine tea under the same name, so read the grade rather than trusting Longzhu alone.
description:
Longzhu Cha comes from Longzhu village in Dunhao, Kaizhou district (formerly Kaixian) in the Three Gorges part of northeast Chongqing, around the Longzhu temple at 800 to 1200 metres. The name means dragon pearl, but this is a strip-shaped green tea rather than a rolled pearl.

Its modern form comes from a revival in the early 1980s, when agricultural officials and tea technicians worked to improve a tea that had been produced for volume rather than quality. The result is tight and downy, with leaves that stay whole.

The cup is a clear greenish yellow with a clean aroma and a sweet, mellow taste that lingers. One local account recommends brewing it with Longjing spring water, which you will probably have to skip. As with other greens, soft, clean water just under boiling will do.

Today it sells as a whole family of grades, including top bud lots, needle and curled styles, everyday green and a jasmine tea. The grade on the pack matters more than the name.
history:
Local gazetteers say tea growing in Kaixian began in the Han and flourished in the Tang, when the official Wei Chuhou wrote a poem on the local Tea Ridge. A Qing prefectural gazetteer praises the Tea Ridge leaf. Promotional accounts claim Longzhu was tribute from the Tang onward, while the county gazetteer more specifically records it being listed as tribute in the fourth year of the Kangxi reign.

The same gazetteer says production was wiped out in the Xianfeng years and revived at the end of the Qing. Output fell badly during the war years, to 140 tonnes for the whole county in 1949, and by the 1970s the county was also making broken black tea.

The Wanxian and Kaixian agricultural bureaus redeveloped Longzhu in the early 1980s. It was rated a quality Sichuan tea in 1983, 1984 and 1985, won a gold at China's second national agricultural fair in 1995, and has since been run as a company-and-farmer operation.
